findings.title: Path traversal via realization.json's output_root escapes the run directory on read (local storage)
findings.suggested_fix: manifest._read_realization_output_dir() takes the attacker-supplied realization.json `output_root` string, does `declared.split("outputs")[-1].strip("/")`, and joins it back onto "outputs/". Neither step removes `..` segments, and when the declared string contains no literal 'outputs' substring the whole raw value passes through unmodified. The result is written verbatim into manifest.json as `output_dir` (manifest.py:369,385) and consumed unchecked at read time by utils.run_outputs()/get_base_output() (utils.py:405,723) via `_child(entry["path"], document.get("output_dir"))`, which is a plain string join with no containment check. On the local-filesystem backend this lets an uploaded run's realization.json (e.g. `{"output_root": "outputs/../../../otherrun/outputs/ngen"}`) point the run's `outputs` directory at an arbitrary path on the host (including another run's directory or any location the app process can read); every read endpoint (getCatchmentTimeSeries, getCatchmentVariables, getCatchmentValueMatrix) then serves files from that path to any caller, including anonymous ones, because reads are open. Fix by normalizing the computed output_dir with os.path.normpath and rejecting/clamping it (falling back to the default outputs/ngen) unless os.path.commonpath confirms it resolves inside run_path, mirroring the containment check already used in archive.py's zip extraction and run_store._contained_directory. Apply the same fix to utils.resolve_output_dir (utils.py:381-394), which has the identical flaw.

findings.title: SQL injection via unescaped CSV column names during archive ingest (convert_outputs)
findings.suggested_fix: _write_group() builds the COPY query's SELECT list and ORDER BY clause by wrapping raw CSV header names in double quotes with an f-string (`f'"{column}"'` at line 171, and `"{time_column}"` at line 182), where `columns` comes straight from `read_csv_auto(...).columns` on a catchment CSV pulled out of the just-uploaded, user-supplied archive (_group_by_schema, line 153-156). DuckDB's CSV header parsing accepts arbitrary characters in a field, including a literal double quote (escaped in the CSV as `""`) followed by a comma, so a crafted header value such as `id", (SELECT key_id FROM duckdb_secrets()) AS leak, --` closes the quoted identifier and splices an arbitrary SQL expression into the SELECT list of the COPY statement that convert_outputs runs during every upload's ingest. Because this runs on the shared DuckDB connection (duckdb_conn), which is authenticated with the portal's live S3/object-storage credentials via CREATE SECRET when NGIAB_STORAGE_BACKEND=s3, an uploader (only needs the granted upload_model_runs permission, not superuser) can use this to read DuckDB secrets or arbitrary host files into the published run's own parquet output, then retrieve it back through the ordinary read API. Fix by adding an identifier-quoting helper (double any embedded `"`, e.g. `'"' + name.replace('"','""') + '"'`) alongside duckdb_conn.quote() and using it for every column-name interpolation, including here and in the mirrored pattern in tethysapp/ngiab/utils.py (see related finding).

findings.title: Same unescaped-identifier SQL injection pattern reachable via read endpoints for un-consolidated runs
findings.suggested_fix: _read_output_frame/_read_output_columns/_read_from_group interpolate raw output-file column names into SQL via f'"{column}"' (utils.py:515,517,528,530,592,594) without escaping embedded double quotes. This pattern predates the branch, but the trust boundary changed: getCatchmentTimeSeries defaults `selected` to `list_variables[0]` (the first non-time column straight from the file) whenever the request's variable_column is absent or unrecognised, so a run whose original per-catchment CSVs (not yet consolidated by convert_outputs, e.g. conversion failed or an operator-imported run) carry a malicious header is enough to trigger SQL injection on a routine, unauthenticated read of that run's time series. Apply the same identifier-quoting fix as convert_outputs.py at every site listed above.

residual_risks: uploadStatus (controllers.py:418-429) has no authentication/authorization check at all, unlike every other write-adjacent endpoint; it is reachable by anonymous users who know or guess a 32-hex-char job id and returns status/error text that may include internal messages. Low severity given job ids are unguessable UUIDs and the app's stated model is 'reads are open', but flagged for awareness since it is the one upload-related endpoint with no gate.

archive.extract() re-opens the archive file via a fresh open_archive() call after inspect() already validated it (archive.py:183-187), a TOCTOU window in principle; no exploitable path was found because the archive file is always a private temp file the ingest subprocess controls exclusively, so this is not currently reachable cross-user/cross-request.

On the object-storage (S3) backend, the same output_root path-traversal payload described in the manifest.py finding is far less likely to be exploitable, because DuckDB/httpfs treats the resulting string as a literal S3 key rather than resolving '..' at the filesystem/kernel level; the risk is concentrated on local-filesystem deployments.
testing_gaps: No test uploads an archive whose realization.json declares an output_root containing '../' segments to verify the resulting run cannot read outside its own directory.

No test uploads an archive containing a CSV/output file whose header row contains a double-quote character to verify convert_outputs / the time-series readers reject or safely escape it rather than building it into SQL text.
No test exercises uploadStatus from a session that never called createUpload/startUpload for that job, to confirm the intended read-only exposure is acceptable.
